scholarly-igem.title.text: iGEM Project; probotic therapy for Parkinson’s treatment

scholarly-igem.para1.text: In iGEM, I worked on the wet lab side—running experiments, generating real data, and helping coordinate the team's bench workflow. Our project focused on engineering microbes to produce levodopa, a first-line treatment for Parkinson's disease, aiming for a more sustainable way to make the drug. I cared about the details: reproducibility, clean data, and making sure our results actually meant something for the rest of the team.

scholarly-igem.para2.text: In Paris, I led a three-person team at the iGEM Grand Jamboree. I ran our seminar, managed the booth, and spent most of the conference translating our science into plain language for judges, researchers, and students passing by. Explaining microbial biosynthesis to a random audience? That was the real challenge—and honestly, the most fun part.

scholarly-immuno.q1.text: We always say “boost immunity”—but do you actually know how the immune system works?

scholarly-immuno.a1.text: It actually has built-in “brakes” to keep itself from going out of control. So here's the question: do you know what happens when immunity loses control?

scholarly-immuno.q2.text: The immune system can kill cancer. So why does cancer still spread?

scholarly-immuno.a2.text: The answer might surprise you: tumors don't fight head-on. They quietly “press” the immune system's brakes.

scholarly-immuno.q3.text: If the immune system is so powerful, why do we still need immunotherapy?

scholarly-immuno.a3.text: Because our understanding of the immune system may be far less than we think. How it balances itself, how it loses control, how tumors exploit it—these are questions science is still working to answer.

scholarly-hir.title.text: HIR writing contest — Harvard International Review academic writing contest

scholarly-hir.a1.text: It sounds simple, but it has no clear definition. In medicine, a disease has a defined population, a measurable endpoint, and a clear outcome. “Healthy aging” has none of these. It is multi-system, gradual, and changes over time—so it is hard to define, evaluate, or commercialize by regular standards.

scholarly-hir.bridge1.text: So if we can’t even define it, how do we prove a treatment works? That’s exactly where the real problem begins.

scholarly-hir.q2.text: Is current medical technology helping us live longer, or live better?

scholarly-hir.a2.text: Mostly longer. Over the past century, human lifespan has been extended, but advanced biomedical innovation still focuses on discrete diseases—one disease, one treatment. The multi-system decline that actually determines whether older people can maintain functional capacity is often treated as less important, because it doesn’t fit the usual standards.

scholarly-hir.bridge2.text: But what if the thing that matters most is exactly the thing our system is worst at measuring?

scholarly-hir.q3.text: Aging isn’t a disease—so how do you treat it?

scholarly-hir.a3.text: That’s the core dilemma. Age-related decline usually shows up as multiple diseases at once. The body loses its ability to clear senescent cells efficiently, and their accumulation damages surrounding tissues. Any treatment must clear the damaging ones while preserving the short-lived senescent cells that support repair. Synthetic biology offers a way to build circuits that respond to the body’s own signals—automatic, precise, and adaptive. But without changing where investment goes, the technology may still end up serving the same old direction.

scholarly-hir.closing.text: So, the science is ready. The question is whether the system is.
